chapters.n: Judges opens just after Joshua’s death. With no single leader, Israel asks the Lord — probably through the high priest — which tribe should lead the fight against the remaining Canaanites.

f.g: Likely through the priest’s Urim and Thummim.

chapters.n: The Lord names Judah, the tribe of future kings, and promises success before the battle begins.
Judah invites Simeon, whose land lay inside Judah’s, to fight together. The brother tribes help each other claim their shares.
The Lord gives Judah victory over the Canaanites and Perizzites at Bezek, a large defeat for the enemy.

f.g: Location uncertain; possibly in the hills west of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: They find and fight Adoni-bezek, whose title means “lord of Bezek.”

f.g: “Lord of Bezek,” a title rather than a personal name.

chapters.n: Cutting off thumbs and big toes made a warrior unable to hold weapons or run. It was a cruel practice of the time.

f.w: cut off his thumbs and his great toes
f.g: A known ancient practice to disable and humiliate captives.

chapters.n: Adoni-bezek admits he did the same to seventy kings, who scrambled for scraps under his table. Even he recognizes that God has repaid him in kind.

f.w: as I have done, so God hath requited me

chapters.n: Judah attacks and burns Jerusalem, but verse 21 shows the Jebusites soon held it again. Israel did not secure the city until David.
Judah campaigns across all three of its regions: the hill country, the southern Negev, and the western foothills.
This retells the capture of Hebron from Joshua 15, now credited to the tribe of Judah as a whole, with Caleb leading.
Judah moves on to Debir, also called Kirjath-sepher.
Caleb promises his daughter Achsah to whoever captures the city.
Othniel captures it and marries Achsah. He is introduced here because he will be Israel’s first judge in chapter 3 — a model of what a good judge looks like.

f.g: Kenaz was the clan father; Othniel was Caleb’s younger kinsman.

chapters.n: Achsah urges her husband to ask for a field, then approaches her father respectfully.
She asks for springs of water to make her dry southern land useful, and Caleb gives generously. A small story of bold, faithful asking.
The Kenites, family of Moses’ father-in-law, move from Jericho with Judah into the southern desert. Outsiders who joined Israel shared in its inheritance.
Judah helps Simeon destroy Zephath and renames it Hormah, “devoted to destruction.”

f.g: Hebrew herem: devoted completely to God, often by destruction.

chapters.n: Judah captures three Philistine coastal cities, though these were later lost; the Greek translation says Judah did not take them.
The Lord was with Judah in the hills, but they could not drive out the plain-dwellers with iron chariots. The deeper question the book raises: was the limit the chariots, or their faith?
Caleb receives Hebron as Moses had promised and drives out Anak’s sons.
Benjamin fails to drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem. From here the chapter becomes a list of failures.
Ephraim and Manasseh (the house of Joseph) march against Bethel, and the Lord is with them.
They send spies to scout Bethel, formerly called Luz.
The spies promise mercy to a man who shows them a way into the city — a scene that echoes Rahab at Jericho.
Bethel is taken, and the man and his family are spared.

f.g: A standard expression for conquest in battle.

chapters.n: Unlike Rahab, this man does not join Israel. He leaves and rebuilds Canaanite Luz elsewhere — a small sign of how Canaanite life simply continued.
Manasseh fails to clear the strong cities of the Jezreel valley, so the Canaanites stay.
When Israel grew strong, they chose forced labor over obedience. This was not inability but compromise.
Ephraim leaves Canaanites in Gezer.
Zebulun leaves Canaanites in two towns but makes them pay tribute.

f.g: Subjects forced to pay or labor.

chapters.n: Asher fails in seven coastal cities, including the major port of Accho and the Phoenician city of Sidon.
Notice the wording: Asher lived among the Canaanites, not the other way around. The Canaanites were the majority.
Naphtali too lives among the Canaanites, though some towns were forced into labor.
Things are worst for Dan: the Amorites pin them in the hills and keep them off the plains. This pressure later drives Dan to migrate north.

f.w: forced the children of Dan into the mountain

chapters.n: The Amorites hold on in Dan’s towns until Joseph’s tribes become strong enough to force them into labor.
The chapter ends by marking the Amorite boundary. The list as a whole shows a conquest left unfinished, preparing the way for the Lord’s rebuke in chapter 2.

f.g: Scorpion Pass, south of the Dead Sea.
Hebrew Sela; possibly a place name.

chapters.n: A messenger of the Lord comes from Gilgal, Israel’s first camp in Canaan, and speaks with God’s own voice: “I brought you out of Egypt… I will never break my covenant with you.” God’s faithfulness is the starting point.

f.g: Hebrew mal’ak, “messenger”; the word can mean a heavenly or an earthly messenger.

f.w: I will never break my covenant

chapters.n: God had told them to make no treaties with the Canaanites and to tear down their altars. They disobeyed, and He asks them to think about why.
Because they disobeyed, God will stop driving the nations out. Those peoples will become thorns in Israel’s side, and their gods a trap.
The people cry aloud at the rebuke. Their sorrow is real, though the coming chapters show it did not last.

f.w: lifted up their voice, and wept

chapters.n: They name the place Bochim, “weepers,” and offer sacrifices. Tears are a beginning, but lasting change requires turning.
The narrator steps back to Joshua’s time, when each tribe went to claim its land. This repeats Joshua 24:28 to set up the pattern of the whole book.

f.w: when Joshua had let the people go

chapters.n: Israel stayed faithful while Joshua and the elders who had personally witnessed God’s miracles were alive.
Joshua, the servant of the Lord, dies at 110.
He is buried on his land at Timnath-heres. The name is spelled with the letters reversed from Timnath-serah in Joshua.

f.g: “Portion of the sun”; Joshua 24:30 has Timnath-serah, “extra portion.”

chapters.n: A whole new generation grows up that does not know the Lord or His works. Faith was not passed on — a warning to every family and congregation.
Here begins the cycle of Judges: Israel sins by worshiping Baal-gods.

f.g: Plural of Baal, “lord” or “master,” the Canaanite storm and fertility god in his many local forms.

f.w: did evil in the sight of the LORD

chapters.n: They abandon the God who rescued them from Egypt for the gods of their neighbors. Forgetting what God has done leads to forsaking Him.
Baal and Ashtaroth were the main Canaanite fertility gods, believed to bring rain and crops — a constant temptation for farmers.

f.g: Plural of Ashtoreth (Astarte), a Canaanite goddess of fertility and war.

chapters.n: Second stage of the cycle: God lets enemies plunder and defeat Israel. Removing His protection is itself a form of judgment.

f.g: Handed them over, like selling a slave.

chapters.n: Wherever they went, things went wrong, exactly as God had warned in the covenant.

f.w: as the LORD had sworn unto them

chapters.n: Third stage: God raises up “judges,” deliverers who rescue Israel. These were more like military champions and leaders than courtroom judges.

f.g: Hebrew shophetim: leaders who “set things right,” delivering and governing.

chapters.n: Even so, Israel kept falling back into idolatry. Scripture often calls idolatry “whoring” because it betrays a covenant like marriage.

f.w: went a whoring after other gods
f.g: Spiritual adultery — unfaithfulness to the covenant God as to a spouse.

chapters.n: God was with each judge, moved with compassion by Israel’s groaning under oppression. “Repented” here means He was moved to pity and changed course — not that He had sinned.

f.g: The Lord was moved with compassion; JST often clarifies passages that speak of God repenting.

chapters.n: When the judge died, Israel went back to idols and got even worse. The cycle is really a downward spiral.

f.w: corrupted themselves more than their fathers

chapters.n: God declares that Israel has broken His covenant and ignored His voice.
So He will no longer drive out the nations left after Joshua’s death.

f.w: I also will not henceforth drive out

chapters.n: The remaining nations become a test: will Israel keep the Lord’s way when temptation is close at hand? Mortality itself is such a test.
So God left those nations in the land, not rushing their removal, even in Joshua’s day.
The narrator lists the nations God left in Canaan. They would test the new generation that had not lived through Joshua’s wars.
A second purpose: each generation had to learn for itself how to fight and trust God. Faith cannot simply be inherited.

f.g: To give them their own experience of relying on God in conflict.

chapters.n: The remaining peoples: the five Philistine city-states on the coast, Canaanites, Sidonians (Phoenicians), and Hivites in the far north.

f.g: Rulers of Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath.
A pass in Syria marking the far northern limit of the promised land.

chapters.n: The test was obedience: would Israel listen to the commandments given through Moses?

f.w: to know whether they would hearken

chapters.n: Israel settles in among six Canaanite peoples instead of standing apart.
Intermarriage leads to idolatry — exactly what Moses and Joshua had warned would happen.
Israel forgets the Lord and worships Baals and Asherah poles. “Forgat” is the key word: neglect, not just rebellion, begins apostasy.

f.g: Hebrew asheroth: sacred wooden poles or images of the goddess Asherah, not literal tree groves.

chapters.n: God hands Israel to Cushan-rishathaim, whose name means “Cushan of double wickedness” — perhaps a mocking nickname. Israel serves him eight years.

f.g: “Doubly wicked Cushan,” likely a play on his name.
Hebrew Aram-naharaim, “Aram of the two rivers,” in northern Mesopotamia.

chapters.n: Israel cries out, and the Lord raises up Othniel, Caleb’s kinsman, as the first judge. His brief story is the model the others are measured against.
The Spirit of the Lord comes on Othniel, empowering him to lead and win. Deliverance comes by God’s Spirit, not mere human talent.

f.w: the Spirit of the LORD came upon him

chapters.n: Forty years of peace follow — about a generation.

f.g: A round number often meaning a full generation.

chapters.n: Israel sins again, and God strengthens Eglon of Moab against them. Even a foreign king can be God’s instrument of discipline.

f.g: His name may suggest “young bull” or “calf”; the story uses it with irony.

chapters.n: Eglon allies with Ammon and Amalek, defeats Israel, and takes Jericho — “the city of palm trees.”
Israel serves Moab eighteen years, sending regular tribute.

f.g: Paid tribute and lived under their rule.

chapters.n: God raises up Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite. Ironically, Benjamin means “son of the right hand.” Ehud carries Israel’s tribute to Eglon.

f.g: Literally “bound in his right hand”; Benjamin was known for left-handed warriors.

chapters.n: Ehud makes a short two-edged dagger, about eighteen inches, and straps it to his right thigh, where guards checking a right-handed man would not look.

f.g: About 18 inches (45 cm); here possibly a shorter cubit.

chapters.n: Ehud delivers the tribute. The note that Eglon was very fat sets up what follows.

f.g: The Hebrew word plays on “fatling,” fitting the calf pun on his name.

chapters.n: After the tribute is delivered, Ehud sends the carriers away.
Turning back at the stone images near Gilgal, Ehud returns alone and asks for a private audience. Eglon sends everyone out.

f.g: Possibly “carved images” or idols — boundary markers near Gilgal.
An order to the attendants: “Quiet!” or “Leave us.”

chapters.n: Eglon sits alone in his cool upper room. When Ehud says he has a message from God, Eglon rises — out of respect or curiosity.

f.g: A cool upper chamber on the roof.
Hebrew davar can mean both “word” and “thing,” a grim double meaning.

chapters.n: Using his left hand, Ehud draws the hidden dagger and strikes.
The vivid detail stresses how completely the oppressor fell. The story is told with the earthy humor of an oppressed people.
Ehud leaves, locking the doors behind him, and slips away.

f.g: Possibly a vestibule or an opening; the Hebrew word is rare.

chapters.n: The servants find the doors locked and assume the king is relieving himself — giving Ehud time to escape.

f.g: A polite way of saying “relieving himself.”

chapters.n: They wait until embarrassed, then unlock the doors and find their king dead.

f.g: Waited until they were uneasy or embarrassed.

chapters.n: Ehud escapes past the stone images to Seirath in the hills.

f.g: A place in Ephraim’s hill country; location uncertain.

chapters.n: In the hills of Ephraim he sounds the trumpet, and Israel rallies to follow him.

f.g: A ram’s horn (shofar) calling men to battle.

chapters.n: Ehud credits the Lord with the victory. Israel seizes the Jordan crossings, trapping the Moabite forces west of the river.
About ten thousand strong, well-fed Moabite soldiers fall, with none escaping.
Moab is humbled and the land enjoys eighty years of rest — the longest peace in Judges.
A brief note on Shamgar, who killed six hundred Philistines with an ox-goad, a long pointed farm stick. God can use humble tools. “Son of Anath” may suggest a non-Israelite background.

f.g: A long wooden pole, often with a metal tip, for driving oxen.

chapters.n: After Ehud dies, Israel again turns to evil. The cycle repeats.
God lets Israel fall under Jabin, a Canaanite king ruling from Hazor in the north. His commander Sisera is the real power in the story.

f.g: Possibly a dynastic name; an earlier Jabin of Hazor fought Joshua.
“Harosheth of the nations,” a site near the Kishon in the northwest Jezreel valley.

chapters.n: With nine hundred iron-fitted chariots, Sisera crushed Israel for twenty years. Israel finally cries to the Lord.
Deborah was a prophetess and Israel’s judge — one of several women scripture honors as prophetesses. She was already judging when the crisis came.
Deborah held court under a palm tree in Ephraim’s hills, where Israelites came for decisions. She was a judge in the courtroom sense as well as a leader.

f.g: A landmark named for her; compare the oak of another Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse.

chapters.n: Deborah summons Barak and delivers the Lord’s command: gather ten thousand from Naphtali and Zebulun at Mount Tabor.

f.g: A rounded mountain rising from the Jezreel plain, a natural rallying point.

chapters.n: The Lord promises to lure Sisera’s chariots to the Kishon River and hand him over to Barak. God sets the stage for victory.

f.g: A seasonal river through the Jezreel valley; when flooded, it turned the plain to mud.

chapters.n: Barak will go only if Deborah comes too. Whether this was weakness or wanting God’s prophet beside him, he trusted her presence.

f.w: If thou wilt go with me

chapters.n: Deborah agrees but warns that the honor will go to a woman. Readers first assume she means herself; the twist comes with Jael.

f.w: sell Sisera into the hand of a woman

chapters.n: Barak musters ten thousand from Zebulun and Naphtali at Kedesh, and Deborah goes with him.
An aside introduces Heber the Kenite, whose clan had moved north apart from the other Kenites. He pitched his tent near Kedesh — setting up the story’s ending.
Sisera learns that Barak has gathered at Tabor. Heber’s family may have been the source of the report.
Sisera brings all nine hundred chariots to the Kishon plain — just where God said He would draw him.
Deborah gives the signal: today is the day, and the Lord has gone out ahead of you. Barak charges down the mountain.

f.w: is not the LORD gone out before thee?

chapters.n: The Lord throws Sisera’s army into panic. The Song of Deborah suggests a storm flooded the Kishon and bogged down the chariots. Sisera abandons his chariot and runs.
Barak pursues the fleeing army back to its base, and the whole force is destroyed.

f.w: there was not a man left

chapters.n: Sisera flees to Jael’s tent, expecting safety since Heber’s clan was at peace with Jabin.
Jael welcomes him warmly and covers him. Hospitality customs made a host responsible for a guest’s safety, which makes her act shocking.
He asks for water; she gives him milk, perhaps to make him drowsy, and covers him again.

f.g: A skin container of milk, likely soured or yogurt-like.

chapters.n: Sisera tells her to stand guard and lie if anyone asks whether a man is inside. The once-mighty general hides behind a woman.

f.g: An irony: soon there will be no “man” there at all.

chapters.n: While he sleeps, Jael drives a tent peg through his temple. Women in nomadic families pitched the tents, so these were tools she knew well.
Barak arrives to find Sisera already dead. Deborah’s prophecy is fulfilled: the honor went to a woman.

f.w: I will shew thee the man whom thou seekest

chapters.n: The narrator credits God: He subdued Jabin that day.
Israel’s power grows until Jabin is destroyed entirely. Chapter 5 celebrates this victory in song.
Deborah and Barak celebrate the victory in song. This poem is considered one of the oldest passages in the Bible, and its archaic Hebrew is hard to translate in places.
The song opens with praise: leaders took the lead and the people volunteered freely. Willing hearts are a theme of the whole poem.

f.g: The Hebrew is uncertain; possibly “when leaders took the lead” or “when locks were loosed” (warriors’ flowing hair).

chapters.n: Deborah calls foreign kings to listen as she sings to Israel’s God. Their power means nothing beside His.
She pictures the Lord marching from Seir and Edom in the south — the region of Sinai — with the earth shaking and clouds pouring rain. The storm at the Kishon was God’s coming.

f.w: when thou wentest out of Seir

chapters.n: Mountains quake before Him, as Sinai did when the law was given. The God of Sinai is the God fighting for Israel now.

f.g: Possibly “the One of Sinai,” a title for God.

chapters.n: Before the victory, roads were too dangerous to use; travelers took back paths. Life under oppression was fearful and hidden.
Village life collapsed until Deborah arose as “a mother in Israel” — a protector and nurturer of the nation.

f.g: Possibly “the peasantry” or “leadership” ceased; the Hebrew is uncertain.

chapters.n: Choosing new gods brought war to their gates. Israel was so disarmed that hardly a shield or spear could be found.

f.g: At the city gates — war at their very doors.

chapters.n: Deborah honors the leaders who volunteered and calls for praise to the Lord.
Everyone — the wealthy who ride white donkeys, those in authority, and ordinary travelers — should tell what happened.

f.g: Light-colored donkeys, ridden by people of rank.

chapters.n: At the wells, once dangerous, people now retell the Lord’s righteous acts. Israel can return to its city gates in peace.

f.g: Wells, where people gathered and where raiders once struck.
Hebrew tsidqot YHWH, His saving acts or victories.

chapters.n: A call to action: wake up, Deborah, and sing! Rise, Barak, and lead away your captives. Scripture later uses “lead captivity captive” for Christ’s victory.
The surviving faithful remnant came down to rule over the powerful. The Lord gave the weak victory over the mighty.
The song now praises the tribes that came: Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir (Manasseh), and Zebulun — even its record-keepers.

f.w: they that handle the pen of the writer
f.g: Possibly officers who held a commander’s staff or scribes who mustered troops.

chapters.n: Issachar’s leaders joined Deborah and rushed into the valley behind Barak. But Reuben debated endlessly instead of acting.

f.g: Long deliberation — much thinking, no action.

chapters.n: A pointed question to Reuben: why stay among your flocks listening to the sheep? They had good intentions but stayed home.

f.g: Sheep pens; possibly campfires or saddlebags.

chapters.n: Gilead, Dan, and Asher also stayed away — busy with land, ships, and harbors. The song names those who didn’t show up.

f.g: Dan may have worked in the coastal shipping trade.

chapters.n: Zebulun and Naphtali risked their lives on the battlefield — they get the highest praise.
The Canaanite kings fought at Taanach by Megiddo’s waters but won no plunder.

f.w: Taanach by the waters of Megiddo
they took no gain of money
f.g: They carried off no silver as spoil.

chapters.n: Heaven itself fought against Sisera. The stars, often linked to rain in ancient thought, joined the battle — a poetic way of saying God sent the storm.

f.g: The stars on their paths across the sky.

chapters.n: The flooded Kishon swept away the enemy. Deborah urges her own soul to march on in strength.

f.w: O my soul, thou hast trodden down strength
f.g: Or “March on, my soul, with might.”

chapters.n: The poem’s rhythm imitates galloping horses fleeing in panic.
A curse on Meroz, a town that refused to help. Failing to stand with the Lord’s cause in a crisis was itself a serious failure.

f.g: An unknown town, probably near the battlefield.

f.w: to the help of the LORD
f.g: To support the Lord’s cause and people.

chapters.n: In contrast, Jael is “blessed above women.” Similar words are later spoken of Mary.
Sisera asked for water; she gave him rich milk in a fine bowl. Hospitality turned into a trap.

f.g: Curdled milk or yogurt, not butter in the modern sense.

chapters.n: Jael grabs the tent peg and workman’s mallet and strikes Sisera through the temple.
The repeated words slow time down as the mighty general sinks and falls dead at a woman’s feet. Some see an echo of the promise that the serpent’s head would be crushed.
The scene shifts to Sisera’s mother at her window, anxiously wondering why her son’s chariot is so late.
Her wise ladies answer, and she repeats their comfort to herself.
They imagine Sisera dividing loot: captive women and embroidered cloth. The irony is painful — the women of Israel were spared because he lies dead.

f.g: Literally “a womb or two,” a crude soldier’s phrase for captive women.

chapters.n: The song ends with a prayer: may God’s enemies perish, but may those who love Him shine like the rising sun. Forty years of peace follow.

f.w: as the sun when he goeth forth in his might

chapters.n: Israel sins again, and the Lord gives them over to Midian, desert nomads from east of the Jordan, for seven years.

f.g: Descendants of Abraham through Keturah; Moses had married into a Midianite family.

chapters.n: Midian’s raids were so harsh that Israelites hid in mountain caves and strongholds.

f.g: Hiding places, perhaps cut into hillsides.

chapters.n: Each year after planting, the Midianites, Amalekites, and other eastern tribes swept in to take the harvest.

f.g: Desert tribes from east of the Jordan.

chapters.n: They camped on the land and ate or destroyed everything as far as Gaza, leaving no food or livestock.
They came like locusts with their camels and herds — too many to count. This is one of the first records of camels used in large-scale raiding.

f.g: Locusts, which strip a land bare.

chapters.n: Israel is reduced to poverty and finally cries out to the Lord.
Israel’s cry is repeated to show it reached God.
Before sending a deliverer, God sends an unnamed prophet to explain why this happened. He begins by recalling the Exodus.

f.g: An unnamed prophet; God first sends correction, then rescue.

chapters.n: God reminds them He rescued them from Egypt and every oppressor and gave them the land.
God had told them not to fear the Amorites’ gods, but they disobeyed. Recognizing sin comes before deliverance.

f.w: fear not the gods of the Amorites

chapters.n: The angel of the Lord sits under an oak at Ophrah while Gideon secretly threshes wheat in a winepress — a pit where the grain would be hidden from raiders.

f.g: Threshing was normally done on open hilltops to catch the wind; a winepress was a sunken pit, good for hiding.

chapters.n: The angel greets him as a “mighty man of valour” — not what he was, but what God saw he could become.
Gideon answers honestly: if God is with us, why is this happening? Where are the miracles our fathers told us about? Scripture allows sincere questions.
The speaker is now called “the LORD.” He doesn’t argue; He sends: “Go in this thy might… have not I sent thee?” God’s call is His answer.

f.g: The angel speaks as the Lord Himself; Latter-day Saints understand Jehovah as the premortal Christ.

chapters.n: Gideon protests that his clan is the weakest in Manasseh and he is the least in his family. God often calls the humble.

f.w: I am the least in my father's house

chapters.n: God promises His presence: Gideon will strike Midian as easily as one man.

f.w: Surely I will be with thee

chapters.n: Gideon asks for a sign that he is truly speaking with God.
He begs the visitor to wait while he brings an offering, and the visitor agrees.
Gideon prepares a young goat, broth, and unleavened bread from about a bushel of flour — a costly gift in a time of famine.

f.g: A dry measure, roughly 20 liters (about half a bushel).

chapters.n: The angel tells him to set the food on a rock and pour out the broth, turning the meal into an offering.

f.g: Another title for the same divine messenger.

chapters.n: With a touch of his staff, fire flares from the rock and consumes the offering, and the angel vanishes. God accepts the sacrifice.

f.w: there rose up fire out of the rock

chapters.n: Gideon realizes who he has seen and is terrified, fearing that no one sees God face to face and lives.
The Lord comforts him: “Peace be unto thee; fear not.”
Gideon builds an altar and names it “The LORD is peace.” The altar still stood when the book was written.
That night God gives Gideon his first mission: tear down his own father’s Baal altar and the Asherah pole beside it. Reform starts at home.

f.g: An Asherah pole, a wooden cult object.

f.w: the second bullock of seven years old
f.g: Seven years may echo the seven years of Midianite oppression.

chapters.n: He is to build a proper altar to the Lord and burn the bull using the wood of the Asherah pole.

f.g: In proper arrangement, or on the stronghold’s top.

chapters.n: Gideon obeys — but at night, afraid of his family and neighbors. His courage is real, if still growing.
In the morning the town sees the Baal altar destroyed and a new altar in use.
They investigate and learn Gideon did it.

f.g: Shows how deeply Baal worship had taken root in an Israelite town.

chapters.n: Shockingly, Israelites demand death for destroying Baal’s altar — the reverse of God’s law, which condemned idolaters.
Joash defends his son with sharp logic: if Baal is a god, let him defend himself. Gideon’s faith may have awakened his father’s.

f.w: if he be a god, let him plead for himself

chapters.n: Gideon is nicknamed Jerubbaal, “let Baal contend,” a standing mockery of Baal’s powerlessness.
The Midianite coalition crosses the Jordan and camps in the Jezreel valley.

f.g: Israel’s richest farmland, a natural target.

chapters.n: The Spirit of the Lord “clothes” Gideon. He blows the trumpet, and his own clan, which had wanted him dead, rallies to him.

f.w: the Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon

chapters.n: Gideon summons Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they come.
Gideon, still uncertain, asks God for confirmation.
He sets out a wool fleece on the threshing floor: let dew fall only on the fleece, and the ground stay dry.

f.g: A sheepskin with the wool still on.

chapters.n: God grants it: by morning Gideon wrings a full bowl of water from the fleece.
Gideon humbly asks again, this time reversing the sign, since wool naturally holds dew.

f.w: Let not thine anger be hot against me

chapters.n: God patiently does it: the fleece is dry and the ground wet. The Lord meets Gideon in his weakness — though faith grows best when we act without demanding more signs.
Gideon’s army camps at the spring of Harod, with the Midianites spread out in the valley below near the hill of Moreh.

f.g: A hill on the north side of the Jezreel valley.

chapters.n: Surprisingly, God says Gideon’s army is too big. If Israel won with a large force, they would boast that they saved themselves. God wants the victory to be clearly His.

f.w: Mine own hand hath saved me

chapters.n: Following the law of Moses, anyone afraid may go home. Twenty-two thousand leave; ten thousand remain.

f.g: Puzzling, since Gilead lies east of the Jordan; some suggest a local hill or a copying change.

chapters.n: Still too many. God will test the men at the water and choose who goes.

f.g: Test, sift — as metal is refined.

chapters.n: At the water, the men are separated by how they drink: those who lap like a dog and those who kneel down.
Only three hundred lapped water from their hands; everyone else knelt to drink. The point is not their skill — God simply chose the smallest group.

f.w: putting their hand to their mouth
f.g: Scooping water to the mouth while staying alert.

chapters.n: God declares He will save Israel with just three hundred men. The others go home.
The three hundred keep the departing men’s supplies and trumpets — which will be their only “weapons.” Midian waits below.
That night God tells Gideon to attack, for the victory is already given.

f.g: Spoken as already done — the certainty of God’s promise.

chapters.n: Knowing Gideon’s fear, God offers encouragement: if you’re afraid, take your servant Phurah and go scout the camp.

f.g: God meets Gideon where he is, without scolding.

chapters.n: Gideon will hear something that strengthens him. He and Phurah creep to the edge of the enemy camp.
The enemy army fills the valley like locusts, their camels like the sand of the seashore.

f.w: as the sand by the sea side

chapters.n: A soldier tells his dream: a round loaf of barley bread rolled into camp and flattened a tent. Barley was a poor farmer’s grain — a picture of humble Israel.

f.g: Barley was cheaper than wheat, food of the poor; Israel was the farming people, Midian the tent-dwellers.

chapters.n: His friend interprets: it is the sword of Gideon. Even the enemy knows God has given Midian to Israel.

f.w: into his hand hath God delivered Midian

chapters.n: Gideon’s first response is to worship. Then he returns, transformed, and rouses his men: the Lord has given you victory.
Gideon divides his men into three companies, giving each a ram’s horn and a clay jar with a torch hidden inside.
“Watch me and do what I do.” Gideon leads by example.

f.w: Look on me, and do likewise

chapters.n: At his signal, they will all blow their horns and shout, “The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon!” God’s name comes first.
They reach the camp just after the guard changes at the middle watch, around midnight, when sentries are least settled. They blow horns and smash jars.

f.g: The second of three night watches, around 10 p.m. to 2 a.m.

chapters.n: Torches flare as the jars break; three hundred horns blare; the shout rings out. In the dark it sounds like a vast army.
Israel’s men simply stand in place, and the enemy camp panics and runs.

f.w: stood every man in his place

chapters.n: In confusion, the Lord sets the enemies against each other. They flee east toward the Jordan.

f.w: set every man's sword against his fellow

chapters.n: Men from the northern tribes join in pursuing the fleeing Midianites.
Gideon calls Ephraim to block the Jordan crossings, cutting off escape.

f.g: Seize the fords and streams ahead of them.

chapters.n: Ephraim captures and kills two Midianite princes, Oreb (“raven”) and Zeeb (“wolf”). Later scripture remembers this as a great deliverance.
The proud tribe of Ephraim angrily complains that Gideon didn’t call them at the start. Jealousy appears even in victory.
Gideon answers with a gentle proverb: Ephraim’s leftover grapes are better than my clan’s whole harvest — your part was greater than mine.

f.g: The leftovers gathered after the main harvest.

chapters.n: Gideon reminds them they captured the Midianite princes. His humble, soft answer calms their anger.
Gideon and his three hundred cross the Jordan, exhausted but still pursuing.

f.g: A phrase often used for enduring when weary.

chapters.n: He asks the town of Succoth, an Israelite town east of the Jordan, for bread for his hungry men.
Succoth’s leaders mock him: have you already captured the kings? They hedge their bets, afraid of Midian’s revenge.

f.w: Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand
f.g: Captors sometimes cut off enemies’ hands as trophies; the officials want proof first.

chapters.n: Gideon vows to punish them with thorns and briers when he returns victorious.
Penuel, where Jacob once wrestled with God, also refuses to help.
Gideon promises to tear down Penuel’s tower when he returns.
The Midianite kings are at Karkor with fifteen thousand men — the remnant of a vast army that had lost 120,000.
Gideon takes the caravan route east and strikes the camp by surprise, while they feel safe.

f.g: The army felt safe and was off guard.

chapters.n: He captures the two kings and routs the army.
Gideon returns from the battle by the pass of Heres.

f.g: Or “by the ascent of Heres,” a place name.

chapters.n: He captures a young man from Succoth who writes down the names of its seventy-seven leaders — a sign that writing was known even among ordinary people.
Gideon presents the captured kings to Succoth, throwing their mockery back at them.
He punishes Succoth’s elders with thorns. “Taught” is a grim irony — they learned a hard lesson.

f.g: Gave a painful lesson; some versions read “threshed.”

chapters.n: He destroys Penuel’s tower and kills the men of the city. Gideon’s methods grow harsh; the story begins to show his darker side.

f.w: slew the men of the city
f.g: A punishment far harsher than his earlier humility suggested.

chapters.n: Gideon asks about men the kings killed at Tabor. They answer: they looked like you — like princes.

f.g: An earlier killing not otherwise recorded.

chapters.n: They were Gideon’s own brothers. This makes the execution a matter of family blood vengeance.
Gideon tells his young son Jether to kill them, but the boy is too afraid. Being killed by a child would have humiliated the kings.
The kings ask Gideon to do it himself, as a man of full strength should. He kills them and takes the crescent ornaments from their camels.
Israel asks Gideon to become a hereditary king. They credit him rather than God — the very danger God warned of in chapter 7.
Gideon gives a noble answer: the Lord shall rule over you. Israel’s true king is God.

f.w: the LORD shall rule over you

chapters.n: But he asks each man for a gold earring from the spoil. The Midianites, like their Ishmaelite cousins, wore gold earrings.

f.g: Here a broad term for desert traders, closely linked to Midianites.

chapters.n: The men gladly throw their earrings onto a spread-out cloak.

f.g: Laid out a cloak to collect the gold.

chapters.n: The gold weighed about 1,700 shekels — around 40 pounds — besides royal jewelry and purple robes.

f.w: a thousand and seven hundred shekels

f.g: Purple dye was costly, worn by royalty.

chapters.n: Gideon makes a golden ephod and sets it up in Ophrah. Israel begins to worship it, and it becomes a trap for him and his family. Even a good man’s well-meant religious object can become an idol.

f.g: A priestly garment or object used to seek God’s will; here it became an object of worship.

chapters.n: Midian never threatened Israel again, and the land had peace for forty years in Gideon’s day.

f.w: lifted up their heads no more

chapters.n: Gideon goes home and lives in his own house — refusing the throne, but living a bit like a king.
He had seventy sons by many wives — the kind of household a king kept.
A concubine in Shechem bears him a son he names Abimelech, “my father is king.” The name hints at ambitions to come.

f.g: A secondary wife of lower status.

chapters.n: Gideon dies at a good old age and is buried in his father’s tomb.
As soon as Gideon dies, Israel turns again to Baal, now worshiping “Baal-berith” — Baal of the covenant — at Shechem. They give their covenant loyalty to a false god.

f.g: “Baal of the covenant,” worshiped at Shechem.

chapters.n: They forget the Lord who had delivered them.
They also show no loyalty to Gideon’s family, setting up the tragedy of chapter 9.
Abimelech, Gideon’s son by a concubine from Shechem, goes to his mother’s relatives to start a campaign for power.
His pitch: would you rather be ruled by seventy sons of Gideon, or by one man — who is also your own kin? He plays on family loyalty and fear.
His uncles spread the message, and Shechem’s leaders lean toward him because “he is our brother.”

f.g: They were persuaded to favor him.

chapters.n: They fund him with seventy silver pieces from Baal-berith’s temple — one for each brother he will kill. He hires reckless, worthless men.
Abimelech murders his seventy half-brothers on a single stone, like a sacrifice. Only Jotham, the youngest, escapes by hiding.

f.g: Possibly a ritual execution, as on an altar stone.

chapters.n: The leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo crown Abimelech by the sacred pillar — the same place where Joshua set up the covenant stone. A sacred place is now used for a crime.

f.w: the pillar that was in Shechem

f.g: Beth-millo, probably a fortress or citadel in Shechem.

chapters.n: Jotham climbs Mount Gerizim, the mountain of blessing above Shechem, and calls out to the city.
Jotham’s parable: the trees decide to anoint a king and first ask the olive tree.

f.g: One of the few fables in scripture; compare 2 Kings 14:9.

chapters.n: The olive declines: why give up producing oil that honors God and people, just to sway over the other trees?

f.g: Rich oil, used in offerings and anointing.

chapters.n: The trees next ask the fig tree.

f.g: A symbol of peace and plenty in Israel.

chapters.n: The fig declines too; its sweet fruit is its true purpose.
Then they ask the vine.
The vine refuses to give up its wine, which cheers God (through offerings) and people. Productive people are busy doing good, not grasping for power.

f.w: wine, which cheereth God and man

chapters.n: Finally the trees ask the bramble — a thorny bush with no fruit or shade.

f.g: A thornbush, probably the buckthorn; good for little but kindling.

chapters.n: The bramble absurdly invites the trees to rest in its shade — and threatens fire if they don’t. Abimelech is the worthless bramble, whose “protection” brings destruction.

f.w: put your trust in my shadow
f.g: An ironic image; a bramble gives almost no shade.
The mightiest trees, standing for Shechem’s leaders.

chapters.n: Jotham applies the fable: if you acted honestly and fairly toward Gideon’s family…

f.w: according to the deserving of his hands

chapters.n: …remember that my father risked his life to rescue you from Midian.
Yet you turned on his house, killed his sons, and made a slave woman’s son king because he is your kin.

f.g: A biting reference to Abimelech’s mother’s lower status.

chapters.n: If you acted rightly, then enjoy your new king — and may he enjoy you.

f.g: Sarcasm: if this was right, then be happy together.

chapters.n: But if not, may fire break out between Abimelech and Shechem and consume them both. This curse frames the rest of the chapter.

f.w: let fire come out from Abimelech

chapters.n: Jotham flees to Beer to escape his brother.
Abimelech rules for three years — a short and violent reign.

f.g: Hebrew “acted as prince”; he was never a true king of all Israel.

chapters.n: God lets a spirit of distrust come between Abimelech and Shechem. Partners in crime turn on each other.

f.g: A spirit of discord or ill will; scripture often attributes to God what He permits.

chapters.n: This was so the murder of Gideon’s seventy sons would be repaid on Abimelech and the Shechemites who helped him.
Shechem’s men set ambushes on the hills and rob travelers, cutting into Abimelech’s income and authority.
Gaal son of Ebed arrives, and Shechem’s people shift their trust to him.

f.g: Ebed means “slave” — perhaps a mocking name.

chapters.n: At the grape harvest festival, they feast in their god’s temple and curse Abimelech.

f.g: Trod the grapes to make wine.

chapters.n: Gaal stirs them up: why serve this son of Gideon? Serve the old Canaanite family of Hamor, Shechem’s founder.
Gaal boasts that if he led the people he would get rid of Abimelech, and he challenges him to come fight.
Zebul, the city’s governor, is angered by Gaal’s words.
Zebul secretly warns Abimelech that Gaal is turning the city against him.
He advises Abimelech to move by night and hide in the fields.
At sunrise, attack; when Gaal comes out, do as you see fit.
Abimelech sets four ambush groups around Shechem overnight.
Gaal stands in the city gate as Abimelech’s men rise from hiding.
Gaal sees men coming down the hills; Zebul mockingly tells him he is seeing shadows, stalling until it’s too late.

f.g: Zebul pretends the shapes are only shadows.

chapters.n: Gaal sees more troops coming from the center and by the Diviners’ Oak.

f.g: Literally “navel of the land,” a high point near Shechem.
“Diviners’ oak,” a tree tied to fortune-telling.

chapters.n: Zebul taunts him: where’s your big mouth now? Go fight the man you mocked.
Gaal leads Shechem’s men out to battle.
Abimelech routs him, with many falling right up to the city gate.
Abimelech stays at Arumah while Zebul expels Gaal from Shechem.
Next day the people go out to the fields, and Abimelech hears of it.
He ambushes them with three companies and attacks.
One group seizes the gate while the others cut down the people in the fields.
Abimelech captures Shechem, kills its people, destroys it, and scatters salt — a symbolic curse of permanent ruin. Jotham’s curse is coming true.

f.g: A symbolic act declaring a place cursed and barren.

chapters.n: Shechem’s tower-dwellers take refuge in the stronghold of El-berith’s temple.
Abimelech learns they have gathered there.
He cuts a branch on Mount Zalmon and tells his men to do as he does — a dark echo of Gideon’s “look on me, and do likewise.”

f.g: A hill near Shechem, perhaps Mount Ebal.

chapters.n: They pile branches against the stronghold and burn it, killing about a thousand people. “Fire from Abimelech” has devoured Shechem, exactly as Jotham said.
Abimelech moves on to Thebez and captures it.
The people flee into a strong tower and climb to its roof.
Abimelech approaches the door to burn this tower too.
A woman drops an upper millstone on his head and cracks his skull. A woman’s hand brings down the tyrant, as with Sisera.

f.g: The upper hand-mill stone women used daily to grind grain.

chapters.n: Dying, he orders his armor-bearer to kill him so no one could say a woman killed him. His pride lasts to the end — and scripture remembers it anyway.
With Abimelech dead, his men go home. His “kingdom” vanishes.
The narrator makes the lesson explicit: God repaid Abimelech for murdering his brothers.
God also repaid Shechem’s men. Jotham’s curse came true; evil that people choose eventually turns back on them.
After the chaos of Abimelech, Tola of Issachar rises to defend Israel. He is one of the “minor judges” whose stories are told only briefly.

f.g: Means “worm” or crimson dye; also the name of an Issachar clan.

chapters.n: Tola judged for twenty-three years — apparently a time of stability after civil war.

f.g: Led and governed, not only in battle.

chapters.n: Jair from Gilead, east of the Jordan, judges next for twenty-two years.
His thirty sons each rode a donkey and ruled a town — signs of wealth and status. The towns were called “villages of Jair.”

f.g: Young donkeys, ridden by people of rank.

chapters.n: Jair dies and is buried in Camon.
Israel’s idolatry reaches a new low: they serve the gods of seven nations and abandon the Lord completely.

f.w: forsook the LORD, and served not him
f.g: Not just adding gods, but dropping the Lord entirely.

chapters.n: God hands them over to two enemies at once: the Philistines in the west and the Ammonites in the east.

f.g: Descendants of Lot, living east of the Jordan.

chapters.n: For eighteen years Ammon crushed the Israelites in Gilead, east of the Jordan.
Ammon even crossed the Jordan to attack Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim.
Israel cries out and, for once, openly confesses: we have sinned by forsaking God and serving Baals.
God answers by reviewing His record: I rescued you from Egypt, the Amorites, the Ammonites, the Philistines.
Also from Sidon, Amalek, and Maon — each time you cried, I saved you.

f.g: Possibly Midianites (as in the Greek Septuagint).

chapters.n: Yet you keep abandoning me, so I will save you no more. God’s patience is not to be taken for granted.

f.w: I will deliver you no more
f.g: A sharp warning meant to bring real repentance, not cheap requests.

chapters.n: With divine sarcasm, God says: go ask your chosen gods to save you. False gods cannot help in trouble.

f.w: Go and cry unto the gods which ye have chosen

chapters.n: Israel surrenders completely: do with us as you see fit, but please save us today. This is real repentance — submission, not bargaining.

f.w: do thou unto us whatsoever seemeth good unto thee

chapters.n: They act: they throw out their foreign gods and serve the Lord. And God could bear Israel’s misery no longer — a tender glimpse of His compassion.

f.w: his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel

chapters.n: Ammon gathers in Gilead; Israel gathers at Mizpeh in Gilead. The stage is set for battle.

f.g: A Mizpah in Gilead, east of the Jordan.

chapters.n: Gilead’s leaders have no champion and offer leadership to anyone who will start the fight — setting up Jephthah’s story.
Jephthah is a brave warrior but an outsider — the son of a prostitute. God often works through people others reject.

f.g: Gilead is both his father’s name and the name of the region.

chapters.n: His half-brothers drive him out so he can’t share the inheritance.

f.g: A woman outside the family — here, a prostitute.

chapters.n: Jephthah flees to Tob, northeast of Gilead, where a band of rough, landless men gathers around him — much like David’s band later.

f.g: A region east of the Jordan, probably in southern Syria.

chapters.n: In time, the Ammonites go to war against Israel.
Gilead’s elders swallow their pride and go to bring Jephthah back.
They ask him to be their military commander.
Jephthah points out the irony: you hated me and threw me out — and now you come to me in trouble?
The elders up their offer: lead us in battle and be head over all Gilead.

f.g: Hebrew rosh, ruler — a higher position than “captain.”

chapters.n: Jephthah negotiates carefully: if the Lord gives me victory, will I truly be your head?

f.w: the LORD deliver them before me
f.g: Jephthah credits success to the Lord from the start.

chapters.n: The elders swear an oath with the Lord as witness.

f.w: The LORD be witness between us

chapters.n: Jephthah is made head and commander, and he repeats the agreement before the Lord at Mizpeh, making it a sacred covenant.

f.w: uttered all his words before the LORD
f.g: Formally confirmed the agreement in God’s presence.

chapters.n: Before fighting, Jephthah tries diplomacy, asking the Ammonite king why he has invaded.

f.w: What hast thou to do with me
f.g: “What quarrel do you have with me?”

chapters.n: Ammon claims Israel stole its land between the Arnon and Jabbok rivers when coming from Egypt, and demands it back.

f.g: Two rivers flowing west into the Dead Sea and Jordan, marking the region east of the Jordan.

chapters.n: Jephthah sends a second, longer message — a careful historical argument.

f.g: Persistence in seeking peace before war.

chapters.n: First point: Israel never took land from Moab or Ammon.
He recounts Israel’s journey from Egypt through the wilderness to Kadesh.
Israel politely asked Edom and Moab for passage and was refused, so it stayed at Kadesh rather than force its way.

f.w: king of Edom would not hearken

chapters.n: Israel went around Edom and Moab, never entering Moab’s territory, which ended at the Arnon.

f.w: Arnon was the border of Moab

chapters.n: Israel asked Sihon, the Amorite king of Heshbon, for passage too.
Sihon refused, gathered his army at Jahaz, and attacked Israel.
God gave Israel victory, and Israel took the Amorites’ land — not Ammon’s.
That is how Israel came to own the land from the Arnon to the Jabbok.
Since Israel’s God gave the land, what right does Ammon have to it?
Jephthah speaks in terms the king would understand: you keep what your god Chemosh gives you; we keep what the Lord gives us.

f.g: Chiefly the god of Moab; Jephthah may treat Ammon and Moab as one claim.

chapters.n: Not even Balak of Moab, who hired Balaam, ever went to war over this land.
Israel had held these towns for three hundred years. Why wait until now to claim them? This rough figure helps scholars estimate the period of the judges.

f.g: A round figure for the time since the conquest.
A town on the Arnon gorge.

chapters.n: Jephthah rests his case: we have not wronged you. Let the Lord, the true Judge, decide between us.
The Ammonite king ignores his reasoning.
The Spirit of the Lord comes upon Jephthah, and he gathers troops through Gilead and Manasseh to attack.

f.w: the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah

chapters.n: Then Jephthah makes a vow, offering God something in return for victory — though the Spirit had already come upon him. He didn’t need to bargain.
He vows that whatever comes out of his house to meet him will be the Lord’s, offered as a burnt offering. The Hebrew can mean “whoever,” a reckless promise in a home where people would come out.

f.g: An offering wholly given to God.

chapters.n: Jephthah fights Ammon, and the Lord gives him victory.

f.g: The victory is credited to God.

chapters.n: He wins a great victory across twenty Ammonite towns, and Ammon is subdued.
Coming home, his only child — his daughter — rushes out dancing to celebrate, as women did after victories. The joy turns instantly to grief.
Jephthah tears his clothes in grief. He feels he cannot take back his vow to the Lord.

f.g: Tore his clothing, a sign of deep mourning.

chapters.n: His daughter shows remarkable faith and courage: keep your vow, since the Lord has given you victory.

f.w: do to me according to that which hath proceeded out of thy mouth
f.g: She accepts the vow’s consequences for her father’s sake.

chapters.n: She asks for two months to go into the hills with her friends to mourn that she will never marry or have children.

f.g: Mourn that she would die, or live, without marriage or children.

chapters.n: He lets her go, and she mourns with her companions in the mountains.

She returns and her father fulfills his vow. Interpreters differ: many think he sacrificed her, which God’s law condemned; others note the stress that “she knew no man” and think she was dedicated to lifelong unmarried service at the sanctuary.

f.w: did with her according to his vow
f.g: The Lord forbade human sacrifice; the text neither approves nor explains the act.

chapters.n: Every year Israel’s young women honored her for four days. The story stands as a tragic warning against rash vows and as a memorial to a faithful daughter.
Ephraim again complains it wasn’t called to fight, just as with Gideon — but this time they threaten to burn Jephthah’s house over him.

f.g: Or “to Zaphon,” a town in the Jordan valley.

chapters.n: Jephthah answers that he did call them, and they didn’t come.
So he risked his life, and the Lord gave him victory. Why attack me now? Unlike Gideon, Jephthah does not soothe their pride.

f.w: I put my life in my hands
f.g: An idiom for risking one’s life.

chapters.n: Civil war breaks out. Ephraim had insulted the Gileadites as runaways and outcasts; the insult helped fuel the fighting.

f.g: A taunt: “You’re just refugees from Ephraim.”

chapters.n: Gilead seizes the Jordan crossings. When fleeing Ephraimites try to cross and deny who they are, they’re questioned.

f.g: Fords, the shallow crossing points of the river.

chapters.n: The password test: “Shibboleth.” Ephraimites’ dialect said “Sibboleth,” giving them away. Forty-two thousand die — a tragic tribal slaughter of Israelites by Israelites.

f.g: Hebrew “ear of grain” or “flowing stream”; today “shibboleth” means a telltale word or custom that marks a group.

chapters.n: Jephthah judges six years, dies, and is buried in Gilead.

f.g: A short tenure, in contrast to earlier judges’ forty years.

chapters.n: Ibzan of Bethlehem judges next — probably the Bethlehem in Zebulun.
Ibzan arranged sixty marriages for his children with outside families, building alliances and wealth. He judged seven years.

f.g: Gave in marriage outside the clan.

chapters.n: Ibzan dies and is buried at Bethlehem.

f.g: Notices of burial show each judge was remembered locally.

chapters.n: Elon of Zebulun judges ten years.
Elon dies and is buried in Aijalon in Zebulun’s land — a different Aijalon from Dan’s.
Abdon of Pirathon in Ephraim is the last of the minor judges.

f.g: From Pirathon, also hometown of one of David’s mighty men.

chapters.n: His forty sons and thirty grandsons rode seventy donkeys — a display of wealth and status. He judged eight years.
Abdon dies and is buried in Ephraim’s hill country. These brief notes give a lull before the long story of Samson.

f.g: A hill area in Ephraim, perhaps once inhabited by Amalekites.

chapters.n: Israel sins again, and the Philistines rule them for forty years — the longest oppression in Judges. Notice that this time Israel doesn’t even cry out for help.

f.g: A sea-people from the Aegean region who settled Canaan’s southern coast, skilled in iron-working.

chapters.n: In Zorah lives Manoah of Dan, whose wife cannot have children. Like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, and Hannah, she will bear a son by God’s gift.
The angel of the Lord appears to the woman and promises she will have a son. God’s message comes first to her, not her husband.

f.w: the angel of the LORD appeared unto the woman

chapters.n: Even during pregnancy she must avoid wine, strong drink, and unclean food, because her son will be set apart from conception.
The son will be a Nazarite from the womb — never cutting his hair — and will begin to rescue Israel from the Philistines. “Begin” is key: David would finish the job.

f.g: From Hebrew nazir, “consecrated” or “separated”; not related to Nazareth.

chapters.n: She tells her husband that a man of God came, awe-inspiring like an angel. She didn’t ask his name.

f.g: A common title for a prophet or messenger.

chapters.n: She repeats the message, adding that the child will be a Nazarite “to the day of his death” — a hint of the story’s end.

f.w: to the day of his death

chapters.n: Manoah prays for the man to return and teach them how to raise the child. A good model: parents seeking God’s help to raise children.

f.w: teach us what we shall do unto the child

chapters.n: God answers Manoah’s prayer, but the angel again appears to his wife in the field while Manoah is away.
She runs to bring her husband.
Manoah follows her and asks if this is the man who spoke to her. He says, “I am.”

f.g: A simple “Yes”; compare the divine name in Exodus 3:14.

chapters.n: Manoah asks how they should raise the boy and what his life will be.

f.w: How shall we order the child
f.g: What rule should govern the child’s life?

chapters.n: The angel simply repeats: let her follow everything I already said.
She must avoid all grape products, wine, strong drink, and unclean food — following the Nazarite rules herself during pregnancy.

f.w: any thing that cometh of the vine

chapters.n: Manoah offers the hospitality of a meal, still thinking the visitor is a man.
The angel declines food but says any burnt offering should go to the Lord. Manoah doesn’t yet understand who he is.
Manoah asks the visitor’s name so they can honor him when the promise comes true.
The angel answers that his name is “secret” — literally “wonderful,” beyond understanding. Isaiah uses the same root for the Messiah: “his name shall be called Wonderful.”
Manoah offers a young goat and grain on a rock to the Lord, and the angel does something wonderful while they watch.

f.g: The same Hebrew root as the “wonderful” name in verse 18.

chapters.n: As the flame rises, the angel ascends in it to heaven. Manoah and his wife fall on their faces in awe.
The angel doesn’t appear again. Now Manoah realizes who he was.
Manoah fears they will die because they have seen God.
His wife reasons wisely: if God wanted to kill us, He wouldn’t have accepted our offering or told us these promises. Her faith steadies his fear.

f.w: If the LORD were pleased to kill us
f.g: She draws comfort from what God has already done.

chapters.n: She names her son Samson, and the Lord blesses him as he grows.

f.g: Probably from Hebrew shemesh, “sun” — perhaps “little sun.”

chapters.n: The Spirit of the Lord begins to stir him in Dan’s camp between Zorah and Eshtaol. His gifts come from God from the start.

f.g: Stir or impel him, like a sudden push.
Hebrew Mahaneh-dan, also a place name.

chapters.n: Samson goes down to Timnath, a Philistine-controlled town nearby, and is attracted to a Philistine woman. The story keeps saying Samson “went down” — physically and spiritually.

f.g: Samson is often driven by what he sees.

chapters.n: He tells his parents to get her for him as his wife. In that culture, parents arranged marriages.

f.w: get her for me to wife

chapters.n: His parents object: why not marry an Israelite instead of an uncircumcised Philistine? Samson insists — literally, “she is right in my eyes,” a phrase that echoes the book’s darkest theme.

f.g: Outside God’s covenant (circumcision was the covenant sign).
Literally “she is right in my eyes.”

chapters.n: The narrator explains that the Lord would use even this to create an opening against the Philistines, who ruled Israel then. God can work through flawed human choices without approving them.

f.g: God turned Samson’s choice into an opportunity; it doesn’t mean God endorsed it.

chapters.n: On the way to Timnath, among the vineyards, a young lion charges Samson. A Nazarite in a vineyard is already in a risky place.

f.g: Nazarites were to avoid all grape products.

chapters.n: The Spirit of the Lord rushes upon him, and he tears the lion apart bare-handed. He tells no one.
Samson talks with the woman and is pleased with her.
Later, returning to marry her, he detours to see the lion’s carcass and finds bees and honey in it.
He scoops out honey and shares it with his parents without telling them its source. Touching a corpse broke his Nazarite vow, and he would have made his parents unclean too.

f.g: Hiding it suggests he knew it was wrong.

chapters.n: Samson holds a wedding feast, probably a drinking party, as was the custom for young men.
The Philistines assign thirty companions — perhaps as guests, perhaps to keep an eye on him.
Samson proposes a bet: solve my riddle during the seven-day feast, and I’ll give you thirty linen garments and thirty sets of fine clothes.
If they fail, they pay him the same. They agree.
The riddle: “Out of the eater came something to eat; out of the strong came something sweet.” For three days they can’t solve it — it depends on his secret.
Desperate, they threaten his bride: get the answer or we’ll burn you and your family. They accuse her of inviting them to rob them.
She weeps and accuses him of not loving her. He answers that he hasn’t even told his parents.
After days of tears and pressure, he tells her, and she passes it on.
Just before sunset on the last day, the men give the answer. Samson replies with a bitter jab: you plowed with my heifer — meaning they used his wife.

f.g: A rude metaphor: you got the answer by using my wife.

chapters.n: The Spirit comes on him, and he kills thirty Philistines in Ashkelon to pay his debt with their clothes. Then he goes home angry.

f.g: A Philistine port about 23 miles (37 km) away.

chapters.n: Samson’s bride is given to his best man — setting up the next round of revenge in chapter 15.

f.w: whom he had used as his friend

chapters.n: At wheat harvest Samson returns with a young goat as a gift to visit his wife, but her father blocks the door.

f.g: Late spring, around May–June, when fields are dry and ripe.

chapters.n: Her father explains he thought Samson hated her, so he gave her to the best man. He offers her younger sister instead.
Samson declares he’ll be blameless this time when he harms the Philistines. The cycle of personal revenge is escalating.
He catches three hundred foxes (or jackals), ties them tail to tail in pairs with torches between.

f.g: Possibly jackals, which roam in packs and are easier to catch in numbers.

chapters.n: He sets the torches ablaze and releases the animals into Philistine grain fields, burning the harvest, vineyards, and olive groves — their whole economy.

f.g: Unharvested grain still in the field; “corn” in KJV means grain.

chapters.n: The Philistines find out why and burn Samson’s wife and her father to death — the very fate she had tried to avoid by betraying him.

f.w: burnt her and her father with fire

chapters.n: Samson vows one more act of revenge, then he’ll stop.

f.g: Revenge rarely stops where we plan.

chapters.n: He strikes them in a great slaughter and hides in a cave in the rock of Etam.

f.g: An idiom for a complete, crushing defeat.

chapters.n: The Philistines invade Judah and spread out at Lehi.

f.g: Hebrew “jawbone”; the place is named for what happens here (verse 17). Unrelated to the Book of Mormon prophet Lehi.

chapters.n: Judah asks why they’ve come. To capture Samson, they say, and pay him back.

f.w: to do to him as he hath done to us

chapters.n: Three thousand men of Judah go to Samson — not to join him, but to rebuke him for provoking their masters. Israel has grown comfortable in bondage.

f.w: Knowest thou not that the Philistines are rulers over us?
f.g: Judah accepts Philistine rule rather than seeking freedom.

chapters.n: They’ve come to tie him up and hand him over. He makes them swear not to kill him themselves.
They agree, tie him with two new ropes, and lead him out of the cave.
As the Philistines shout in triumph, the Spirit of the Lord rushes on Samson; the ropes melt like burnt flax and fall away.
He grabs the fresh jawbone of a donkey and kills a thousand men. A fresh bone was hard and heavy; touching a dead animal again was another breach for a Nazarite.
Samson composes a victory chant with a pun: in Hebrew, “donkey” and “heap” sound alike.

f.g: Hebrew hamor (donkey) and hamor (heap) — a wordplay.

chapters.n: He throws away the jawbone and names the place “Jawbone Hill.”
Desperately thirsty, Samson prays for the first time on record. He acknowledges the victory came from the Lord.
God splits open a hollow, water flows, and Samson revives. He names the spring “the spring of the one who called.” God answers even an imperfect servant who calls on Him.
Samson judged Israel twenty years under Philistine domination — he never fully freed them.

f.w: in the days of the Philistines
f.g: While the Philistines were still in power.

chapters.n: Samson goes to Gaza, a major Philistine city, and visits a prostitute. Once again, what he “saw” leads him astray.

f.g: The southernmost of the five Philistine cities.

chapters.n: The Gazites learn he is there, surround the city, and wait quietly at the gate to kill him at dawn.
At midnight Samson rips out the city gate — doors, posts, and bar — and carries it to a hill facing Hebron, nearly forty miles away. A city’s gate symbolized its strength; he humiliates Gaza.

f.w: took the doors of the gate

f.g: The heavy crossbeam that locked the gate.

chapters.n: Later he falls in love with Delilah in the valley of Sorek. She is the only woman in Samson’s story who is named — and the only one he is said to love.

f.g: “Valley of the choice vine,” between Israel and Philistia.
Her name may relate to “flirtatious” or “delicate”; her nationality isn’t stated.

chapters.n: Each of the five Philistine lords offers her 1,100 silver pieces — a fortune — to discover the secret of his strength.

f.g: 5,500 shekels in total — an enormous sum.

chapters.n: Delilah asks him plainly what makes him strong and how he could be tied up.
Samson toys with her: tie me with seven fresh bowstrings.

f.g: Fresh, moist cords or bowstrings made from animal gut.

chapters.n: The Philistines supply the cords, and she binds him.
With men hiding in the room, she cries out. He snaps the cords like burnt string.

f.g: Coarse fiber from flax, which burns easily.

chapters.n: Delilah complains he has mocked her and lied.
He offers another false answer: new, unused ropes.
Again she binds him and calls out, and again he snaps them like thread. He doesn’t seem to see the danger he’s playing with.
She presses again. This time his answer comes dangerously close to the truth — his hair.

f.w: the seven locks of my head

chapters.n: She weaves his hair into the loom and pins it, but he wakes and pulls away the whole loom.

f.g: The peg that tightens the loom.

chapters.n: She uses the same emotional pressure as his first wife: how can you say you love me when your heart isn’t with me?

f.w: How canst thou say, I love thee

chapters.n: She nags him day after day until he is sick to death of it.

f.g: Worn out to the point of despair.

chapters.n: He finally tells her everything: his hair has never been cut because he has been a Nazarite from birth. His strength wasn’t magic in the hair — it came from his covenant with God, which the hair represented.

f.w: There hath not come a razor upon mine head

chapters.n: Delilah knows this time it’s true and calls the lords, who come with the money.
She lulls him to sleep on her lap and has his seven locks shaved. His strength leaves him.
He wakes, assuming he’ll shake free as always — not realizing the Lord had left him. One of scripture’s saddest lines: we can lose the Spirit without noticing.

f.w: the LORD was departed from him

chapters.n: The Philistines gouge out his eyes and set him to grinding grain in prison — work for slaves and animals. The man led by his eyes loses them.

f.g: A common punishment for prisoners of war.

chapters.n: A quiet note of hope: his hair begins to grow back. God has not finished with him.

f.g: A sign of renewal and the possibility of returning to God.

chapters.n: The Philistine lords hold a great festival to their god Dagon, crediting him with Samson’s capture.

f.g: A major Philistine god, probably associated with grain.

chapters.n: The crowd praises Dagon when they see Samson. The contest is now between the Lord and Dagon.
Celebrating and drunk, they bring Samson out to entertain them — mocking him — and stand him between the pillars.

f.g: Entertain us, possibly by being mocked.

chapters.n: Samson asks the boy leading him to let him feel the pillars that hold up the building.
The temple is packed, with all the lords inside and about three thousand people on the roof watching.

f.g: Archaeology shows Philistine temples had central pillars supporting the roof.

chapters.n: Samson prays: Lord God, remember me and strengthen me just this once. Even his motive is mixed — revenge for his eyes — yet God hears a humbled man’s plea.

f.g: Hebrew Adonai YHWH — Samson addresses God with deep reverence.

chapters.n: He grips the two central pillars, one in each hand.
“Let me die with the Philistines.” He pushes with all his might, and the temple collapses. In death he defeats more enemies than in life.

f.w: Let me die with the Philistines

chapters.n: His family recovers his body and buries him in his father’s tomb, between Zorah and Eshtaol — where the Spirit first stirred him. He judged Israel twenty years.
The book’s last section (chapters 17–21) leaves the judges behind to show how far Israel had fallen. It begins with an ordinary man named Micah in Ephraim’s hills.

f.g: Means “Who is like the LORD?” — ironic for a man about to make an idol. Not the later prophet Micah.

chapters.n: Micah confesses to his mother that he stole her 1,100 shekels of silver — the same sum each Philistine lord paid Delilah. He returns it, apparently scared by her curse, and she quickly turns it into a blessing.

f.g: Pronounced a curse on the unknown thief.

chapters.n: His mother says she had dedicated the silver to the Lord — to make an idol! This confused mix of Lord-worship and idol-making shows how badly Israel had forgotten the law.

f.w: a graven image and a molten image
f.g: A carved image and a cast metal one — forbidden by the second commandment.

chapters.n: Though she “wholly dedicated” the silver, she gives only two hundred shekels to a silversmith. Even her devotion is half-hearted.
Micah builds a private shrine with an idol, an ephod, and household gods, and makes his own son a priest — though only Aaron’s descendants could be priests.

f.g: Household idols, sometimes used for divination.
Literally “filled the hand of,” the term for ordaining a priest.

chapters.n: The theme of the book’s ending: no king, and everyone did what seemed right to them. Without the Lord’s rule, people made religion up as they went.

f.w: every man did that which was right in his own eyes

chapters.n: A young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah enters the story. Levites were supposed to live in Levite cities and serve God, not drift.
He leaves Bethlehem to live wherever he can find a position, and arrives at Micah’s house.

f.w: where he could find a place
f.g: Looking for work or a better situation.

chapters.n: Micah asks where he’s from, and the Levite explains he is looking for a place to settle.
Micah hires him as his “father and priest” for ten shekels a year, clothing, and food. The priesthood becomes a paid job for a private shrine.

f.g: “Father” was a title of respect for a spiritual adviser.

chapters.n: The Levite is content, and Micah treats him like one of his sons.
Micah “ordains” the Levite himself — authority he did not have. Priesthood can’t be bought or conferred by just anyone.
Micah is sure the Lord will bless him now that he has a Levite. He thinks having the right religious pieces guarantees blessing, while ignoring God’s commandments.

f.w: Now know I that the LORD will do me good
f.g: A false confidence based on outward forms.

chapters.n: Again, no king in Israel. The tribe of Dan had never secured its assigned land and goes looking for somewhere else to live.
Dan sends five scouts from Zorah and Eshtaol — Samson’s home area. On the way they lodge at Micah’s house.
They recognize the Levite’s voice — perhaps his southern accent — and ask what he is doing there.
He explains that Micah hired him as his priest.

f.g: In such and such a way.

chapters.n: They ask him to inquire of God whether their mission will succeed.
He gives a vague, pleasing answer: “Go in peace; the Lord is watching your way.” It sounds spiritual but commits to nothing.

f.w: before the LORD is your way
f.g: Ambiguous: could mean “approved” or simply “seen” by God.

chapters.n: At Laish in the far north they find a peaceful, unguarded, isolated people with no allies nearby — an easy target.
They return to report to their people.
They urge an attack: the land is excellent; don’t be lazy. Their words sound like Joshua’s — but they’re aimed at a peaceful town outside the Lord’s assignment.

f.g: Are you just going to sit there?

chapters.n: They claim God has given it to them — based on the Levite’s vague words.
Six hundred armed Danites set out.
They camp near Kirjath-jearim; the spot was later called “Camp of Dan.”
They come to Micah’s house in Ephraim.
The scouts tell the others about Micah’s idols and ephod and hint they should take them.

f.w: consider what ye have to do
f.g: A hint: think about what you should do.

chapters.n: They approach the Levite’s quarters and greet him.

f.g: Greeted him, asked how he was.

chapters.n: The six hundred armed men wait at the gate, intimidating.
The scouts go in and take the idols, ephod, and household gods while the priest is distracted at the gate.

f.g: Stealing gods that couldn’t protect themselves.

chapters.n: The priest asks what they’re doing.
They tell him to be quiet and come with them: isn’t it better to be priest to a tribe than to one household?

f.w: lay thine hand upon thy mouth

chapters.n: The priest is delighted with the promotion and carries the idols himself. His loyalty goes to the highest bidder.
They leave with children, livestock, and goods in front — protecting them from any pursuit from behind.
Micah’s neighbors gather and chase after the Danites.
The Danites turn and ask Micah what’s wrong with him, bringing such a crowd.
Micah cries: you took my gods that I made, and my priest — what do I have left? The irony is plain: gods that can be stolen are no gods at all.
The Danites threaten him: keep quiet, or hot-tempered men will kill you and your family.
Outmatched, Micah goes home empty-handed — losing what he once stole and misused.

f.g: Might makes right in this lawless time.

chapters.n: The Danites attack peaceful Laish, kill its people, and burn the city.

f.w: a people that were at quiet and secure
f.g: The text stresses the victims’ innocence and helplessness.

chapters.n: No one came to rescue Laish; it was isolated. The Danites rebuild and settle there near Beth-rehob.

f.g: A region in the far north near Mount Hermon.

chapters.n: They name the city Dan after their ancestor. It became Israel’s northern border town: “from Dan to Beer-sheba.”

They set up the idol and make Jonathan, a grandson of Moses’ son Gershom, their priest. Hebrew manuscripts raise a letter to change “Moses” to “Manasseh,” likely to spare Moses’ name the shame. His line served this shrine until the Assyrian exile.

f.g: The Hebrew has a raised letter n; without it the name reads “Moses.”

chapters.n: Micah’s idol stayed at Dan the whole time the true house of God was at Shiloh. Dan later became a center of Jeroboam’s golden calf worship.

f.w: house of God was in Shiloh

chapters.n: Another story from the time with no king. A Levite in Ephraim’s hills takes a concubine — a secondary wife — from Bethlehem. This is one of the darkest chapters in scripture, recorded to show how far Israel had fallen.

f.g: A legal wife of lower status, often without a dowry.

chapters.n: She is unfaithful to him (or, in some ancient versions, becomes angry with him) and returns to her father’s home for four months.

f.g: The Greek Septuagint reads “became angry with him.”

chapters.n: He follows her to win her back with kind words. Her father welcomes him warmly.
The father-in-law urges him to stay, and he remains three days feasting.
On the fourth morning, the father presses him to eat before leaving. Hospitality customs made it hard to refuse.
They eat and drink together, and the father urges another night.
He gives in and stays again.
The fifth day repeats the pattern; they linger into the afternoon.
As evening comes, the father asks him once more to stay and leave early tomorrow.

f.w: the day groweth to an end

chapters.n: This time the Levite refuses and leaves late, reaching Jebus (Jerusalem) by evening.
With the day nearly over, his servant suggests spending the night in Jebus.
The Levite refuses to stay in a foreign city and insists on reaching an Israelite town, expecting safety among his own people. Bitter irony follows.
He aims for Gibeah or Ramah, Benjamite towns a few miles north.

f.g: Later the hometown and capital of King Saul.

chapters.n: They reach Gibeah of Benjamin at sunset.

f.w: the sun went down upon them
f.g: Night falls — a darkness both literal and moral.

chapters.n: They sit in the town square, but no one offers them a place — a serious breach of hospitality.

f.w: no man that took them into his house

chapters.n: An old man, himself an outsider from Ephraim, comes in from the fields. Only the stranger shows kindness.
He sees the travelers and asks where they are going and from where.
The Levite explains his journey and that no one has taken them in.

f.g: Possibly the sanctuary at Shiloh; the Septuagint reads “my house.”

chapters.n: He makes clear they have their own food and fodder; they only need shelter.

f.g: Female servant — here politely meaning his concubine.

chapters.n: The old man welcomes them and insists they not sleep in the street — he knows the town’s danger.

f.w: let all thy wants lie upon me
f.g: I will take care of whatever you need.

chapters.n: He brings them in, feeds the animals, and offers the customary foot-washing and meal.
As they relax, wicked men surround the house, pound on the door, and demand the guest for sexual assault. The scene deliberately echoes Sodom: Israel has become like Sodom.
The host goes out and begs them not to commit this wicked outrage against his guest.

f.g: Hebrew nebalah, a shameful outrage against God’s moral law.

chapters.n: Horrifyingly, the host offers his own daughter and the concubine instead. The text records this without approving it; it exposes how corrupt even “hospitable” people had become.
The mob refuses. The Levite pushes his concubine outside, and the men abuse her all night. Scripture records this crime plainly so that readers will grieve and condemn it.

f.w: when the day began to spring

chapters.n: At dawn she collapses at the door of the house where her husband was.

f.g: Her husband — the title makes his failure to protect her more striking.

chapters.n: In the morning he opens the door to leave and finds her lying with her hands on the threshold — a heartbreaking image of a victim reaching for safety that never came.

f.g: The doorway — the boundary of protection she couldn’t cross.

chapters.n: He coldly tells her to get up. There is no answer; he places her on the donkey and goes home.

f.g: The Greek adds “for she was dead.”

chapters.n: He cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel — a shocking summons to the tribes, like Saul’s later call to arms.
All who see it say nothing like this has happened since the Exodus. They call for counsel and action. Some evils demand that a community stop, think, and respond.

f.w: consider of it, take advice, and speak your minds
f.g: Think about it, take counsel, and speak up.

chapters.n: All Israel — from Dan in the north to Beer-sheba in the south, plus Gilead — gathers at Mizpeh before the Lord. Ironically, this crime unites them as no judge did.

f.g: The full length of the land, north to south.

chapters.n: The tribal leaders assemble with 400,000 foot soldiers.

f.w: assembly of the people of God
f.g: Israel acting as a covenant community.

chapters.n: Benjamin hears of the gathering but doesn’t attend. Israel asks how this crime happened.

f.g: Tell us how this evil happened.

chapters.n: The Levite begins his account of the night in Gibeah.

f.g: The narrator names her a murder victim.

chapters.n: He says the men meant to kill him and raped his concubine until she died. He leaves out that he pushed her outside himself.

f.g: His version shapes the story to his own advantage.

chapters.n: He explains why he sent her body throughout Israel: because of this outrage.
He calls on all Israel to decide what to do.
Israel vows that no one will go home until this is dealt with.
They agree to choose by lot who will attack Gibeah.
One in ten soldiers will handle food supplies for the army so the campaign can be sustained.
