All Israel gathers against the city, united.
They first send messengers to Benjamin demanding an explanation — the right first step.
They ask only for the guilty men so they may “put away evil from Israel,” as the law requires. Benjamin refuses, protecting criminals out of tribal loyalty.
Instead Benjamin musters its towns at Gibeah to fight the rest of Israel. Civil war begins.
Benjamin has 26,000 soldiers plus 700 elite fighters from Gibeah.
Seven hundred left-handed slingers could hit a hair without missing. Slingers were deadly in ancient warfare.
The rest of Israel numbers 400,000 — a huge mismatch on paper.
Israel asks God at Bethel which tribe should lead. Judah is named first — echoing the book’s opening, but now against a brother tribe.

f.g: Hebrew Beth-el; possibly the town of Bethel, where the ark then was.

chapters.n: Israel camps against Gibeah.
They form battle lines.
Benjamin charges out and kills 22,000 Israelites the first day.
Israel rallies and lines up again in the same place.
They weep before the Lord and ask whether to fight their brother again. The Lord says go. Notice they now see Benjamin as a “brother.”

f.g: A growing awareness of the tragedy of civil war.

chapters.n: On the second day they advance again.
Benjamin kills 18,000 more. Why did God allow defeat? Many see a lesson: Israel too needed humbling and purifying before acting as God’s instrument.
All Israel goes to Bethel, weeps, fasts all day, and offers burnt and peace offerings. Only now do they turn to the Lord with full humility.

f.g: Fellowship offerings shared in a meal before God.

chapters.n: They ask the Lord again, for the ark of the covenant was then at Bethel.
Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson, served before the ark — showing these events happened early in the judges period, though placed at the end of the book. This time the Lord promises victory.

f.w: to morrow I will deliver them
f.g: For the first time, God promises success.

chapters.n: Israel sets an ambush around Gibeah — the same tactic Joshua used at Ai.
On the third day Israel lines up as before.

f.g: Just as before — to make Benjamin overconfident.

chapters.n: Benjamin comes out, is drawn away from the city, and kills about thirty Israelites along the roads.
Benjamin thinks it’s winning again, while Israel pretends to flee to lure them farther out.

f.g: A planned retreat, a feigned flight.

chapters.n: The main army regroups at Baal-tamar while the ambush rises from near Gibeah.

f.g: “Lord of the palm,” a site near Gibeah.
Possibly “the open area west of” Gibeah.

chapters.n: Ten thousand elite troops strike Gibeah; the fighting is fierce. Benjamin doesn’t yet see the disaster coming.
The narrator gives the summary first: the Lord struck Benjamin, and 25,100 fell. Verses 36–46 then retell the battle in detail.
Here is how it happened: Israel gave ground on purpose, trusting the ambush.
The ambush rushes into Gibeah and strikes the city.
The signal was a great column of smoke rising from the city.
Benjamin, killing about thirty, thought it was the first battle all over again.
Then the Benjamites look back and see their city going up in smoke.

f.g: Literally “the whole city went up” — as an offering of smoke.

chapters.n: Israel turns to fight, and Benjamin is terrified, realizing disaster has come.
They flee toward the wilderness but are caught between the two Israelite forces.

f.g: The fighting caught up with them.

chapters.n: Israel surrounds and crushes them east of Gibeah.
Eighteen thousand brave Benjamites fall.
Survivors flee to the rock of Rimmon; five thousand more are cut down on the roads and two thousand at Gidom.

f.g: Picked off, like gleaners gathering leftover grain.
A cliff or cave area east of Bethel.

chapters.n: In total about 25,000 Benjamite soldiers die — the summary figure in round numbers.
Only six hundred men survive, hiding at the rock of Rimmon for four months. A whole tribe hangs by a thread.
Israel then destroys Benjamin’s towns, people, and animals. Justice has turned into near-genocide of a brother tribe — vengeance gone too far, which chapter 21 must try to repair.

f.w: set on fire all the cities

chapters.n: In the heat of anger at Mizpeh, Israel had sworn never to let their daughters marry Benjamites. Now that rash oath threatens to wipe out a tribe.

f.g: A rash vow, like Jephthah’s, that creates new problems.

chapters.n: The people go to Bethel, sit before God until evening, and weep bitterly.

f.g: Bethel, where the ark was then kept.

chapters.n: They ask the Lord why one tribe is now missing from Israel — though the answer lies in their own choices.

f.g: The twelve tribes were meant to stay whole.

chapters.n: Next morning they build an altar and offer burnt and peace offerings, seeking God’s help.

f.g: A temporary altar for this occasion.

chapters.n: They ask who failed to come to Mizpeh, since they had also sworn death on anyone who stayed away.
Israel grieves for Benjamin as a brother — one tribe has been cut off.
Their dilemma: how to find wives for the six hundred survivors without breaking their oath.
They discover that no one from Jabesh-gilead, east of the Jordan, came to the assembly.

f.g: A town in Gilead; later closely tied to Saul, a Benjamite.

chapters.n: A roll call confirms it.
Israel sends twelve thousand warriors to destroy Jabesh-gilead. One rash oath is used to get around another, at a terrible human cost.
They are to kill all males and all married women — sparing only unmarried girls.
Four hundred young women are taken to the camp at Shiloh.
Israel offers peace to the Benjamite survivors at the rock of Rimmon.
The Benjamites return and receive the four hundred women, but two hundred men are still without wives.
Israel grieves that the Lord had allowed a gap in the tribes.

f.g: A gap, as in a broken wall.

chapters.n: The elders ask again how to provide wives for the rest.

f.w: the women are destroyed out of Benjamin

chapters.n: They agree a tribe must not vanish from Israel; the survivors need a future.

f.g: A continuing family line and land.

chapters.n: But they still feel bound by their oath not to give daughters to Benjamin.

f.g: The curse they pronounced on themselves.

chapters.n: They remember a yearly festival to the Lord at Shiloh, giving careful directions to its location — suggesting the sanctuary was little visited in those days.

f.g: Perhaps a harvest festival, such as Tabernacles.

chapters.n: They tell the Benjamites to hide in the vineyards.
When Shiloh’s young women come out to dance, each man is to seize one and carry her home. Technically no father “gave” a daughter — a legal loophole that ignored the women’s will.
The elders plan to calm the angry fathers and brothers: since they didn’t give their daughters, they haven’t broken the oath.

f.w: Be favourable unto them for our sakes
f.g: Be gracious to them as a favor to us.

chapters.n: The Benjamites do it, take wives, return home, and rebuild their towns. Benjamin survives — later producing King Saul and, much later, the Apostle Paul.
The assembly breaks up and everyone returns home.

The book closes with its verdict: no king, and everyone did what was right in their own eyes. Without the Lord as true King in their hearts, Israel fell into chaos — preparing for the call for a king in Samuel and, ultimately, for the righteous King, Jesus Christ.

f.w: every man did that which was right in his own eyes
